Empirical Research Plan ― “Deep Determinants of Comparative Development”

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Cross-sectional two–stage least squares (2SLS) / limited–information maximum likelihood (LIML) instrumental-variables (IV) estimation.

Why IV?
• The key regressors – contemporary institutional quality (I) and trade integration (T) – are plausibly endogenous: richer societies may develop better institutions and trade more (“reverse causality”); un-observables (culture, history) may affect both Y and the deep determinants (omitted-variable bias).  
• Geography (G) is taken as exogenous but also belongs on the right-hand side because it may raise income directly (transport costs, disease burdens).  
• History provides strong, interpretable, external instruments that shift I or T but are unlikely to affect current income except through those channels.  
• A single cross-section of 80–140 countries means DID/RDD/event-study designs are infeasible.

Baseline structural equation (logged variables, lower case):
y_i = α + β₁ i_i + β₂ t_i + β₃ g_i + X_i′ γ + ε_i                        (1)

Endogenous regressors   i_i , t_i  
Exogenous deep determinant g_i (absolute latitude or tropical land share)  
Controls X_i : continent dummies, legal origin, religion fractions, etc.

First-stage system:
i_i = π₀ + π₁Z_Ii + π₂Z_Ti + π₃g_i + X_i′δ + u_i                    (2a)  
t_i = θ₀ + θ₁Z_Ti + θ₂Z_Ii + θ₃g_i + X_i′κ + v_i                    (2b)

Main instruments  
• Z_I (institutional): log European settler mortality; shares speaking English / other European languages; dummies for French, British, Spanish legal origin  
• Z_T (trade): Frankel-Romer predicted trade share (gravity residual); log distance to major markets; landlocked indicator

The over-identified system lets us test for instrument validity and compare the relative magnitudes of β₁, β₂, β₃.

2. Treatment and Control
Because treatment is continuous we speak of “higher” vs. “lower” levels.

Treatment variables  
• i_i  = Kaufmann–Kraay–Zoido rule-of-law index (1998)  
• t_i  = average trade share 1950-1998 (imports+exports over GDP)

Control group (counterfactual)  
• Countries that, owing to historical/instrumental variation, have exogenously lower values of i_i or t_i while holding geography constant.

Timing  
• Instruments refer to colonial era (16th–19th century) or long-run geography; outcome measured in 1995. No discrete event date is needed.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A1 Instrument relevance: Z_I strongly predicts i_i; Z_T strongly predicts t_i after conditioning on geography/controls.  
Plausibility: Settler mortality and language shares are powerful predictors (shown in AJR 2001; Hall-Jones 1999). Gravity-based trade share also highly correlated with actual openness.

A2 Exclusion restriction: Instruments affect contemporary income only through their impact on institutions or trade, not directly or through omitted channels.  
Plausibility: Debatable but defensible if we (i) control flexibly for geography and colonizer fixed effects, (ii) show that instruments are uncorrelated with alternative channels (human capital, capital deepening) once I and T are conditioned on.

A3 Linear additivity and no interaction omitted (unless modeled).  
We will later explore interaction terms (e.g., I × G) but baseline assumes additive separability.

A4 No weak-instrument bias: first-stage F-statistics > 10 (or Cragg-Donald > 10 for multiple endogenous regressors). LIML and Anderson-Rubin tests used as robustness.

A5 Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): One country’s institutional quality or trade share does not directly change another’s income (after controlling for trade share already). Reasonably plausible at the aggregate level.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
Threat 1 Exclusion violation – settler mortality may proxy for disease environment that still depresses income today via health, not just institutions.  
Fix: (i) Control for malaria ecology, mean temperature, disease prevalence; (ii) Include human-capital and health-capital controls; (iii) Use over-identification tests; (iv) Show robustness dropping Sub-Saharan Africa.

Threat 2 Weak or multi-collinear instruments – Z_I and Z_T might be correlated, diluting power.  
Fix: (i) Report Sanderson-Windmeijer weak-instrument F-stats for each endogenous variable; (ii) Use LIML or Fuller(1) estimator; (iii) Combine instruments into optimally weighted indices to increase strength.

Threat 3 Omitted confounders correlated with both determinants and income (e.g., culture, early state formation).  
Fix: Include rich set of controls (religion shares, World Polity indicators, pre-1500 population density); run Oster (2019) or Altonji-Elder-Taber style exercise to test sensitivity; show placebo regressions on pre-colonial income where available.

5. R Code Outline
```r
# install.packages(c("readr","dplyr","fixest","sandwich","lmtest","AER"))
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(fixest); library(AER); library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data
dat <- read_csv("country_data.csv")   # user supplies

# 2. Construct variables
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    lgdppc95   = log(gdppc_ppp_1995),
    inst       = ruleoflaw,                     # KKZL index
    trade      = (exports + imports)/gdp,       # average 1950-98 already provided
    abs_lat    = abs(latitude),                # geography
    sett_mort  = log(settler_mortality),        # instrument 1
    pred_trade = frankel_romer_pred,            # instrument 2
    eng_share  = frac_english,                  # instrument 3
    europ_lang = frac_other_euro_lang,
    landlock   = landlocked,
    distance   = log(distance_world_markets),
    controls   = factor(region)                 # simple example
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(lgdppc95), !is.na(inst), !is.na(trade))

# 3. Main 2SLS regression
iv_form <- lgdppc95 ~ inst + trade + abs_lat | 
           abs_lat + eng_share + europ_lang + sett_mort + 
           pred_trade + distance + landlock

mod2sls <- ivreg(iv_form, data = dat)
coeftest(mod2sls, vcov = vcovHC(mod2sls, type="HC1"))

# First-stage F-statistics
summary(mod2sls, diagnostics = TRUE)

# 4. Robustness: LIML estimator with fixest
mod_liml <- feols(lgdppc95 ~ inst + trade + abs_lat | 
                  abs_lat + eng_share + europ_lang + sett_mort + 
                  pred_trade + distance + landlock,
                  data = dat, 
                  iv = "liml")
etable(mod2sls, mod_liml, se = "hc1")

# 5. Over-identification Hansen J
diagnostics <- summary(mod2sls, diagnostics = TRUE)$diagnostics
print(diagnostics[c("Sargan", "Wu-Hausman"), ])
```

6. Expected Results
Prior from existing literature:  
• β̂₁ (institutions): positive and economically large. A 1-point increase in rule-of-law (≈½ s.d.) should raise log GDP per capita by roughly 0.8 → about +80 % in levels.  
• β̂₂ (trade): smaller but positive. A 10 ppt increase in trade share (≈1 s.d.) raises income by perhaps 0.05–0.10 log points (5–10 %).  
• β̂₃ (absolute latitude): once I and T are instrumented and included, coefficient may fall toward zero, indicating geography’s direct effect is weak.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV context)
C1 Instrument relevance              1  
C2 Instrument exclusion              0.5 (some concerns)  
C3 No weak-instrument bias           1 (confirmed via F-stats)  
C4 Correct functional form           1 (logs, linearity plausible)  
C5 No missing channels/SUTVA         0.5 (spillovers possible, but minor)  
Total = 4/5 – reasonably credible but still dependent on exclusion assumption.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
